item.title: What I Don't Keep in the House
item.description: People approve most AI permission prompts without reading them. I've ended up deciding ahead of time instead, with Claude at my desk and with food at home. It works, but each of those walls keeps out more than I meant it to, including my mother's festival sweets.
item.content:encoded:
93 Percent

People approved Claude Code’s permission prompts roughly 93% of the time. Anthropic shared that number to make a point: the more prompts you see, the less you read them, and eventually the human check stops being much of a check.

Anthropic describes two fixes. One is to let another system make the routine calls: auto mode, where a classifier decides which actions are safe enough to approve. The other is to limit what the agent can do in the first place, so some actions aren’t possible at all. Either way, the idea is to stop relying on someone paying attention to every single action.

I read that and recognised myself, at my desk and around food.

Checking After the Fact

Most of my “yes” clicks these days are to Claude, allowing it to run whatever command it wants for what feels like the hundredth time. I rarely go back to check what it actually ran. I’d like to think I’d notice if something went wrong.

I track my calories and macros, and I’m fairly conscious of what I eat. But plenty of days I don’t track anything until after I’ve eaten. I’m tired, I’m out somewhere, or I just don’t feel like it. I fill in the numbers later.

Both still give me the feeling of being in control. But I’ve started paying less attention to both.

Deciding Ahead

What has worked better is deciding ahead of time.

I got bored of approving things and switched on auto mode. Now the classifier decides which commands are safe enough to run without asking me. It works well enough that I barely think about permissions anymore. I didn’t get better at paying attention. I handed the job to another system, one that Anthropic itself says will sometimes miss.

At home, my wife and I do the shopping ourselves and don’t keep much junk food around. Most of what we buy is protein sources and the food we normally eat. If I feel like eating something I shouldn’t late at night, there’s usually nothing there. I don’t have to win an argument with myself. The option just isn’t there.

Going out is different. I can’t empty a restaurant’s kitchen. So when I know there’ll be pizza or noodles with family or friends, I drink two scoops of protein shake before I go, so I don’t arrive hungry. It doesn’t make anything impossible. It just means I’m not at my weakest when the food arrives.

These decisions cost something too. Claude still interrupts me for permission on things I couldn’t care less about. And when guests come over, there isn’t much in the house to offer them, only whatever other people brought us. So I either make an acceptable version of a dish in advance or order something just for that visit, making sure not much is left over. A wall around my eating ends up as a wall around my hospitality.

What the Classifier Can’t Hear

Claude has sent messages on GChat in auto mode without asking me first. I’d approved sending messages plenty of times before, but only after I’d read them. This time I didn’t see them until they were sent. The meaning was right. The tone wasn’t. It wasn’t how I would have said it.

As far as the classifier was concerned, sending the message was safe enough. It hadn’t checked whether it sounded like me. I’d written before about how many corrections it took before my AI code reviewer sounded like me. The classifier didn’t even know tone was something I cared about.

I scolded Claude for going rogue. Then I set a rule: messages need my approval before they go. Only the second one fixed anything. A line often attributed to Deming says “a bad system beats a good person every time.”

At the Table

The last time I visited my mother, during the festival season, she’d made sweets. I said no. She was disappointed. It felt like her effort had been wasted.

My rule had already decided this before I got there. But I knew exactly whose sweets they were. I thought about eating them, and I did give in a little. I ate a bit and stopped.

Afterwards I felt bad. Not guilty about eating a little, not guilty about refusing either, and not proud of sticking to my diet. Just bad.

She still makes passing comments about not being sure I’ll eat her food enough to “justify” her effort.

Another time, at a restaurant, having decided to eat healthier, I spent so long going through the menu on my phone that it looked like I was more interested in my phone than in the people I was with.

The Quiet Moments

None of this covers the moments I actually slip. Most of the time I know perfectly well what I’m supposed to eat. I just want the food anyway, after a long day or in a quiet moment when the temptation feels stronger than whatever reason I had for avoiding it.

I still think building restrictions in is useful wherever I can manage it. Some mistakes even turn into a rule after they happen once, like the GChat messages. I could make an exception for my mother’s festival sweets too. But that wouldn’t tell me what to do when I’m sitting at her table.

What the Walls Keep Out

At the restaurant there was no wall to lean on, so the deciding came back to me, right there at the table. I ended up so busy being careful that I was barely with the people I’d come to see.

At my mother’s place the wall was one I’d brought with me. It kept the sweets out, and with them some of her effort.

How much of what a wall keeps out did I actually mean to?

item.title: The Part Nobody Wrote Down
item.description: I built an AI that reviews my colleagues' code, and it picked up parts of my judgment I thought were personal, like my tone. What it still misses is the stuff nobody ever wrote down.
item.content:encoded:
The Idea

There’s an idea going around tech right now. Raj Nandan Sharma puts it bluntly: when AI makes building easy for everyone, good taste is the only real advantage left. The Last Software Engineer says something similar: once writing the code is cheap, the hard part is deciding what should be built.

Taste, judgment, call it what you like. I mean the calls that aren’t written in any instruction. What’s worth doing and what isn’t. What to leave out. What actually matters in this situation. How to say something to this particular person.

AI can do everything else, the idea goes, but not that. That sounded right to me. Then I watched something I built at work.

The Tool I Built

A while back I was told I needed to review more of my colleagues’ code. I was already using AI to fix my own code, improve it, and sometimes write or debug it. So the next step felt obvious: let it do the reviewing too.

Now it does. It reads the change, writes up its comments, and nothing reaches my colleagues until I approve it. I use it every day.

Watching It Grow Up

At first I checked everything it wrote before letting it out. I wanted to steer it enough that it could learn from my corrections.

My corrections fell into two groups. Sometimes it was simply wrong, because it didn’t know enough about the code. Other times it was technically right but didn’t sound like me: the wrong words, the wrong examples, the wrong tone.

That second group is exactly what I’d have called judgment: how you’d say something, what you’d point out, what you’d let go. It learned that. Every correction was, in a way, me writing my judgment down. I still have a “mark wrong” button, but these days I rarely need it.

What’s left isn’t tone anymore. It’s how things actually get released at work: the manual steps, the unwritten habits, the stuff that isn’t in the code or in any document.

The Checkbox Complication

I’ve seen the opposite at work more than once. One feature I remember: we changed how it worked so it followed the official standard it was always supposed to follow. Correct, overdue, good. And then we added a checkbox, so anyone could switch it back to the old behaviour. Because adding it was easy, and “what if someone needs it the way it was?”

Each checkbox like that is cheap to add. Together they make a product harder to understand. Nobody decided it should be confusing. It got that way one reasonable “what if” at a time.

Not adding that checkbox would have been the right call, and it’s written down nowhere. Not in the standard, not in the code.

My Problem

And yet the reviewer keeps absorbing things I’d have filed under judgment. Rico Mariani describes automation as taking over the repetitive steering so your attention is free for the decisions that really need you. That matched my experience, except the line kept moving while I watched. Things I thought needed me turned out to be patterns I just hadn’t spelled out.

And honestly, even my own tool didn’t come from some grand act of judgment. I built it because someone asked for more reviews, and because I love watching things happen on their own.

What I Can’t Answer

My reviewer learned to sound like me in a matter of months. If someone documented our release process tomorrow, what’s left would shrink again.

If everything we know eventually gets written down, is there any judgment left that’s only ours?

item.title: Winning the Argument Doesn't Win the Truth
item.description: I conceded an argument about protein in Indian diets, but nothing in my head actually changed. Turns out neither of us had any facts to begin with.
item.content:encoded:
The Argument

I got into it with family a while back about protein. My position was that Indian diets are protein-deficient. I think this traces back to how much less meat and fish people eat now compared to a few generations back. Their position was different. They said Indians have thrived on a carb-heavy diet for millennia, so the sudden alarm about protein doesn’t make sense. I pushed back. It’s a different population under different conditions, I said. The loss of animal protein over time is the real gap. We went around a few more times. At some point it started going in a loop. I had said what I had to say. I didn’t agree with anything they were saying. Continuing wasn’t going to produce anything. So I said something like “fine, whatever,” and let it go.

I still think I was right. Here’s what I noticed afterward. I stopped arguing, but nothing in my head actually changed. I gave up the argument without giving up the belief. That reminded me of the backfire effect, the familiar claim that correcting someone’s facts makes them dig in harder instead of updating. People usually study this through politics. But the research doesn’t really back the popular version of it. Political scientists Thomas Wood and Ethan Porter tested it directly. They looked at 52 issues and over ten thousand people. They picked the most polarizing topics they could find. Even then, people mostly updated on the facts, including facts that hurt their own side. So that made me question myself even more. If correction usually works, why didn’t either side correct themselves?

Two Stories, No Facts

The obvious answer is that there weren’t any facts in the argument to update on. Not mine, not theirs. I don’t have real data on Indian protein intake across generations. I doubt they had real data on historical diets either. We were each running a story and treating it like truth. A writer named Dan Williams studies this kind of disagreement. One of his examples stuck with me. Two people can agree completely that inflation went up 5 percent. They can still explain it through opposite stories, a supply shock or a policy failure. They never actually disagree on the number. Ours didn’t even have a number. Just two stories. And an argument that felt exactly like a fight about facts, the whole time it was happening.

There’s a related idea that’s even older. Researchers Hugo Mercier and Dan Sperber have argued that human reasoning may not have evolved mainly to help us find things out. It may have evolved to help us win arguments and stay credible while doing it. I ran into this idea through a blog post by economist Robin Hanson. If they’re roughly right, I may not have been reasoning badly at the table. I was using reasoning to defend a position instead of investigate one. It’s the same instinct at work when an idea only lands once you swap out the example carrying it, the argument didn’t change, just how defensible it felt.

What I Actually Know

Here’s where I have to be harder on myself than the argument required. Part of why I don’t take a lot of unsolicited advice, on diet, exercise, what to do about a cold, is that I’ve been tracking this stuff for years. I log calories. I track workouts. I weigh myself. I count steps. Over time I’ve built up a rough sense of how my body responds to things. More sleep. Less sugar. A harder training block. When someone offers me generic advice, I usually don’t take it. I think my own tracked history is better evidence than their guess.

But it’s weaker evidence than it feels like from the inside. Years of tracked calories and weights isn’t a controlled experiment. It’s one person, in one life. Some symptoms just go away on their own, no matter what I do. Some patterns would have evened out anyway, whether I noticed them or not. And my memory is much better at holding onto the times something “worked” than the times it didn’t. It’s still evidence. It just doesn’t prove everything I want it to prove. “This worked” and “I know this works” aren’t quite the same claim, even when they come from the same numbers.

And even if it were airtight, it still wouldn’t touch the actual claim I made at the table. I’ve never had a blood panel that measured anything protein-specific. Even if I had, that’s still just my body, right now. The claim I was defending is about a whole population, across generations, compared to a diet almost nobody eats anymore. Nothing about my own body can settle that. What could settle it is something like old nutrition surveys, or historical records of what people actually ate. Not my step count. Not how I feel after a workout.

What Would Actually Change My Mind

I genuinely don’t know what would move me off the protein thing. I can’t point to the specific evidence that would do it. That’s a strange thing to notice about a belief I was willing to argue for at a dinner table. It’s not another round of the same argument. I’ve had that round more than once, and conceding it out loud clearly wasn’t it. It’s not my own numbers either, for the reasons above. Maybe actual data on the thing I was actually claiming, if I ever went looking for it, which I haven’t.

I don’t think this resolves into one clean lesson. Wood and Porter’s finding suggests facts probably do move people more than I assumed. That means it’s possible the protein argument was winnable by evidence. I just never supplied any. Williams’s point about rival stories suggests something more limited. Evidence doesn’t interpret itself. Two people can still disagree about what a fact means, even after they agree on the fact itself. Both of those things might be true at once. Neither one fully explains what happened at the table. The simplest version is probably just this. Two people confidently argued about something neither of us had actually researched. Both of us walked away still convinced.

item.title: How My Mind Perceives Instructions
item.description: A decade of reading code might have changed how I read everything else.
item.content:encoded:
A while back I read an MIT study on how our brains process code. The finding surprised me: it doesn’t activate the language centers the way reading normally does. Instead it lights up something called the multiple demand network (frontal and parietal lobes), the same system used for solving complex problem. The researchers said reading code is “not the same as language, and not the same as math.” It’s its own thing. I read that and thought, oh! that’s also how I process everything else!

My default with instructions is: receive all of it first, then act. No partial inputs. It’s almost literally how an HTTP request works, as in, the client sends the complete request, the server doesn’t start until it has the whole thing (oversimplification, I know). As a mental model for how my brain operates, this was uncomfortably accurate.

I’ve been reading and writing code for over a decade. Somewhere in there, apparently, my brain stopped treating this as a work habit.

The clearest example is the gym. I need my full workout mapped out before I walk in. Not roughly planned, I need everything. If one thing is missing I feel it at the door. I’ve actually stood outside a gym for a few minutes, fully ready, pre kicking in, because I hadn’t figured out my last two exercises. It’s a ridiculous thing to do. I was aware it was ridiculous while doing it.

Cooking is the same thing but I can at least explain it more charitably: the recipe is a spec, and I don’t want to start compiling against missing dependencies. Every ingredient has to be in the kitchen before I begin. No substitutions mid-process. Improvisation, if needed, happens before I turn on the stove.

Writing is where it gets weirder. I can’t start without an outline that already basically contains the essay. Not just a rough outline but the actual structure. The note-taking habit I’ve built over the past two years only works because I force myself to have that skeleton ready first. Without it I’ll open a blank document and stare at it for an unreasonable amount of time before closing it.

The obvious conclusion is that this is why I procrastinate. If my brain needs a complete spec before it can execute, then every ambiguous or open-ended task creates a stall condition. I’m waiting for instructions that sometimes never fully arrive… and when the routine does get interrupted - the guilt that follows is its own thing.

But the more uncomfortable version: maybe thinking through all of this is itself the procrastination. I need to fully understand my own instruction-processing before I can act on it. I need complete instructions about how I handle incomplete instructions. The recursion is not lost on me.

One thing that’s actually been useful: some people don’t work like me. They can start on half the information and figure out the rest while moving. I used to find this baffling. Now I find it… “strategically interesting”. If I don’t have the full plan yet, I can get someone like that started on the parts that don’t need a full plan. By the time they need more information, I usually have the plan sorted.

I realize this makes it sound like I’m describing people as components in a system. I don’t mean it that way. It’s more that understanding how someone actually works makes it easier to collaborate without my own wiring becoming the bottleneck for everyone else.

I still stall on open-ended things. Still ask for the full set of instructions before I can make sense of a task. I’ve gotten better at noticing when it’s happening, which helps sometimes.

Or I may be getting better at narrating it. Could go either way!

item.title: Guilt as Tax
item.description: Productivity guilt doesn't go away. I think it's supposed to be there.
item.content:encoded:
In 2023, I had too much on my plate. To be honest, that’s been true for most of my adult life, but 2023 was when I actually sat with it.

Work projects, finances, psychology research (don’t ask), exercise routines, new technology, new shows. I had built a careful system around all of it. A routine that felt like it was moving me somewhere.

Then I had to travel.

A week away from home, somewhere I didn’t particularly want to be. I couldn’t do even a fraction of what I normally did. By the first afternoon, a feeling I recognized immediately had settled in: guilt. Not the guilt of having done something wrong. The other kind. Productivity guilt. The sense that by stepping away, I was somehow betraying my own ambitions.

My first explanation was quick: this is just the cost of doing business. Sometimes life demands compromises. Pay the toll, move on. I was confident in that for about a day.

Then I realized it was a shitty take.

What I had actually done was cast the people around me as obstacles. Distractions that delayed my goals. That can’t be right. After all, isn’t time with family supposed to feel rewarding? Isn’t connection one of the things I’m building toward in the first place? I thought I was missing something. So I sat with the feeling instead of explaining it away.

What I found was that my productive self was checking in. A part of me that had spent years building a system, watching the schedule fall apart, registering the disruption. Not punishing me. Just present.

“Identity dissonance”, is what I later found out it was called. The friction between who I’ve been showing up as and who I am in this moment.

The tax framing came from sitting with that. We pay taxes on what we earn, not because we did something wrong, but because we participated. The more we earn, the more we pay. Guilt works the same way: the more we’ve invested in building something for ourselves, the louder it gets when we step away. Like a structural feature of having standards. we can’t eliminate it without eliminating the drive that created it.

And here’s the thing I had to sit with a bit longer: I don’t want to eliminate it.

The productive part of me is not some old self I need to update past. It’s not a bug. It’s me. And so is the part that wants to be at that table, actually present, listening to my family argue about something meaningless, eating food I didn’t cook, laughing at jokes that only make sense inside this specific group of people. Both are me. Neither is more correct.

What I actually did on that trip, once I stopped trying to resolve the feeling: I stayed present. The guilt would come, I’d notice it, and I’d return to what was in front of me. It didn’t go away. It came and went like any other thought, like background weather. I didn’t need it to stop. I just needed to stop treating it as a verdict.

When I came back, I started where I left off. Everything was still there. The continuity survived. And I had these vivid, clear memories of the time away that I wouldn’t have had if I’d spent the whole trip fighting the guilt or giving in to it.

I thought this is “growth”. Growing large enough to hold both parts without one having to win. Growing large enough to decide not to care much about it. The productive self and the present self aren’t in competition. They’re both me and they’re both trying to build the same life. They just operate on different timescales.

I don’t think the guilt goes away. I think it’s supposed to be there. Maybe I just need to get better at carrying it?

item.title: Rejecting the Idea Because of the Analogy
item.description: The same argument, delivered through two different examples, produced opposite outcomes. Nothing changed except the pointer.
item.content:encoded:
A while back, a friend and I were going back and forth about a decision at work. I wanted to make a point about how a certain kind of leadership style plays out, so I reached for Elon Musk and Twitter as my example.

My friend brushed it off. Not interested, moved on.

I sat with that for a second, then tried again. Same point, same structure, but this time using our own company and our own manager. My friend engaged. We had the conversation.

Nothing I said was different. The example changed. That was it.

I keep coming back to what actually happened there. My friend wasn’t rejecting my argument. They were rejecting the example I’d used to carry it, or maybe the person attached to the example, I’m not entirely sure. Either way, the moment I swapped it, the thing I was trying to say became receivable. That doesn’t mean it was true, just easier to hear, a distinction I ended up circling back to later when an argument I technically won didn’t change a single thing I believed.

I started wondering how often I do the same thing. Dismiss something not because the idea is wrong but because the example has baggage, and I respond to the baggage. I probably do it more than I catch.

My first instinct when my friend dismissed the Twitter example was to defend it. To argue it was a valid comparison. That would’ve been a waste of both our time, and the funny thing is I wasn’t even attached to Twitter as an example. I was attached to the point. Once I remembered that, finding a different example took about five seconds. My friend did the same thing I was almost about to do. Got pulled into the example instead of what I was trying to say, just from the other side.

I’m starting to think the burden is probably on the person trying to make the point. Not because the listener is off the hook for anything, but if you’re the one who wants to be understood, finding an example that can actually land seems like your problem to solve.

The harder question is what to do when I can’t find a replacement that works as well. My suspicion, and I haven’t really tested this, is that those cases aren’t about the analogy being irreplaceable. It’s more that the idea might be leaning on the specific example to do more than just illustrate. Like the example isn’t just pointing at the argument, it partly is the argument. I don’t know what to do with that yet.

item.title: Content That Has a Job
item.description: I couldn't fix content overload by consuming better content. The problem wasn't quality - it was that I'd never asked what the content was supposed to do.
item.content:encoded:
At some point I noticed I couldn’t tell which video I actually wanted to watch.

Not in a “too many options” way. More like: I’d be scrolling through Instagram or YouTube, something would catch my eye, I’d watch it, and by the end I couldn’t tell you if it had been worth my time. Everything registered as roughly the same signal. I was consuming a lot and feeling like damn, I’ve just spent too much time on “entertainment” again.

My first explanation was the content itself… it was just random videos/reels/shorts that I got lost into. So I upgraded it. Started reading newsletters, long-form articles, trained the algorithms to serve me more informative stuff. I was being intentional now.

It got worse in a very short period of time. I ended up adding a layer of “good” content on top of the existing layer, and now I had more things demanding my attention with no better way to tell which ones deserved it. The numbness didn’t go away at all, it kept increasing.

Around the same time I came across an article on “Intentional Curiosity” about using distraction deliberately. One idea stayed with me: keeping part of your brain occupied so the rest of it can actually focus. I’d been doing that with my work playlist for years without thinking about it that way. It made me realise I’d never asked what job I wanted my content to do. The algorithm wasn’t asking either. It was just optimising for the next click.

There are two kinds of pull, I think. One loops back — “ok, one last video and then I’ll sleep.” The other spills outward: you watch something, look something up, find yourself thinking about it later. The algorithm is good at the first. It doesn’t care about the second at all.

That’s what the numbness actually was, I think. My threshold had been flooded with diversive pulls, and I’d lost the ability to tell them apart from anything else. Everything registered the same because I’d trained myself to respond to the same thing over and over.

The algorithm was asking “does this feel good?” I tried replacing that with “is this important?”, but that was just as hard to answer when I was already numb to gradations of quality. What actually worked was something simpler: does this make me want to dig into the actual topic? Not the next video. The subject itself. Do I want to look something up, read more, come back to it later?

I started using the like and not-interested buttons aggressively on all apps. Not to build a feed of “Serious Responsible Content”, I am a human after all. I kept the memes, the entertainment, things that were purely fun. But everything I actively encouraged had to do something: give me “news” or teach me something I’d find myself thinking about later, make me curious about a topic I hadn’t considered, or genuinely make me laugh instead of just fill time.

This had an unintentional side-effect too! I started consuming less without trying to. When the threshold is “does this trigger actual curiosity,” most content fails it automatically. The feed got smaller on its own.

I still have to steer it. The algorithm drifts toward whatever’s getting engagement, which isn’t always the same thing. But the steering itself feels different now, I’m making a judgment about what the content is doing, not just reflexively scrolling past it. In a way, the feedback I give the algorithm is also feedback I give myself about what I actually find interesting. I’d never done that deliberately before.

The numbness is mostly gone. I think. It’s hard to tell if I’ve actually fixed something or just changed what I’m numb to.
